title: Speed up a slow builder ten times

blocks.text: A transmission operator (fictional) assigns one-week line inspections to weeks. Its builder, `build_slow` in `inspections.py`, is correct and has been reviewed against the formulation, but it takes minutes on a full year of tasks: every lookup in it scans a whole DataFrame. Your job: make it at least ten times faster, and prove the models are identical.

The model, with $`J`$ the tasks, $`S_j`$ the weeks task $`j`$ may use, $`W`$ the weeks of the capacity table, $`h_j`$ the crew-hours of task $`j`$, $`v_j`$ its value and $`C_w`$ the capacity of week $`w`$:
The data is three DataFrames: `tasks` (`task`, `hours`, `value`), `options` (`task`, `week`, one row per variable) and `capacity` (`week`, `hours`).

Write `build_fast(tasks, options, capacity)` so that `build_fast(...).export_model()` equals `build_slow(...).export_model()`: the same variables with the same names in the same order, the same rows in the same order with the same bounds and coefficients, and the same objective. Read `build_slow` closely for the order it creates things in, and for what it does when a week or a task has nothing to sum. Any approach that makes the identical model passes: lookups built once (dictionaries, `groupby`), `mathopt.fast_sum`, or a `ModelProto` built from arrays.

The tests check identity only, never speed, because a speed test would fail on a busy machine. Run the file to measure the speed-up on 1,500 tasks; the reference is several tens of times faster than `build_slow` there, and your number will differ. About fifteen lines.

from __future__ import annotations

import random
import statistics
import time

import pandas as pd
from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


def build_slow(tasks: pd.DataFrame, options: pd.DataFrame, capacity: pd.DataFrame) -> mathopt.Model:
    """The team's builder: correct, and slow, because every lookup scans a whole table."""
    model = mathopt.Model(name="inspections")
    y = {}
    for _, o in options.iterrows():
        y[o.task, o.week] = model.add_binary_variable(name=f"y_{o.task}_{o.week}")
    for _, t in tasks.iterrows():
        weeks = options[options.task == t.task]["week"]                     # scans every option
        model.add_linear_constraint(mathopt.LinearExpression() + sum(y[t.task, w] for w in weeks) <= 1,
                                    name=f"once_{t.task}")
    for _, c in capacity.iterrows():
        load = mathopt.LinearExpression()
        for _, o in options[options.week == c.week].iterrows():              # scans every option
            hours = tasks[tasks.task == o.task]["hours"].iloc[0]             # scans every task
            load += float(hours) * y[o.task, o.week]
        model.add_linear_constraint(load <= float(c.hours), name=f"crew_{c.week}")
    objective = mathopt.LinearExpression()
    for _, o in options.iterrows():
        objective += float(tasks[tasks.task == o.task]["value"].iloc[0]) * y[o.task, o.week]
    model.maximize(objective)
    return model


def build_fast(tasks: pd.DataFrame, options: pd.DataFrame, capacity: pd.DataFrame) -> mathopt.Model:
    """The same model as build_slow, built with lookups made once."""
    model = mathopt.Model(name="inspections")
    hours = dict(zip(tasks["task"], tasks["hours"]))
    value = dict(zip(tasks["task"], tasks["value"]))
    by_task, by_week, terms = {}, {}, []
    for task, week in zip(options["task"], options["week"]):
        var = model.add_binary_variable(name=f"y_{task}_{week}")
        by_task.setdefault(task, []).append(var)
        by_week.setdefault(week, []).append(float(hours[task]) * var)
        terms.append(float(value[task]) * var)
    for task in tasks["task"]:
        model.add_linear_constraint(mathopt.fast_sum(by_task.get(task, [])) <= 1, name=f"once_{task}")
    for week, cap in zip(capacity["week"], capacity["hours"]):
        model.add_linear_constraint(mathopt.fast_sum(by_week.get(week, [])) <= float(cap), name=f"crew_{week}")
    model.maximize(mathopt.fast_sum(terms))
    return model


def instance(n: int, seed: int = 1) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """A made-up instance: n one-week inspection tasks, each allowed in up to three of 12 weeks."""
    draw = random.Random(seed)
    tasks = pd.DataFrame({"task": [f"T{i:04d}" for i in range(n)],
                          "hours": [draw.randint(4, 40) for _ in range(n)],
                          "value": [draw.randint(1, 90) for _ in range(n)]})
    rows = [(t, w) for t in tasks["task"] for w in sorted(draw.sample(range(1, 13), draw.randint(1, 3)))]
    options = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["task", "week"])
    capacity = pd.DataFrame({"week": range(1, 13), "hours": [draw.randint(200, 900) for _ in range(12)]})
    return tasks, options, capacity


if __name__ == "__main__":
    tasks, options, capacity = instance(1_500)
    same = build_fast(tasks, options, capacity).export_model() == build_slow(tasks, options, capacity).export_model()
    print("identical models:", same)
    ratios = []
    for _ in range(3):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        build_slow(tasks, options, capacity)
        slow = time.perf_counter() - start
        start = time.perf_counter()
        build_fast(tasks, options, capacity)
        ratios.append(slow / (time.perf_counter() - start))
    print(f"build_fast is {statistics.median(ratios):.0f}x faster on 1,500 tasks (median of 3 rounds; "
          "your machine's number will differ)")

cases.says: on a small instance the fast builder's exported model equals the slow builder's
on a generated instance of 200 tasks the exported models are equal
a week in the capacity table that no task may use still gets its capacity row
capacity rows come in the order of the capacity table, even when it is not sorted
a task with no allowed week still gets its once row, with no terms
variables are created in the order of the options table, even when it is not sorted

origin.section: A Fast Builder Is Correct Only If Its Exported Model Equals the Slow One's

concepts: a faster builder is accepted only when its exported model equals the reference builder's
a ModelProto filled from arrays becomes a model through Model.from_model_proto, and its rules are the builder's to keep
